newsitem.title: LATVIA: Interview - Lithuania finmin reassures on election.
newsitem.headline: Interview - Lithuania finmin reassures on election.

text.p: Lithuanian Finance Minister Algimantas Krizhinauskas said on Thursday that a swing to the right after October 20 elections would lead to few major changes in the country's economic path, even in the key currency.

The ruling Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), a party of former Communists, is expected to be beaten in the elections and a centre-right coalition led by the Homeland Union of independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis to take power.
An area the Homeland Union has touched on is its opposition to the currency board system of regulating the litas currency.
But Krizhinauskas also said he did not foresee any sudden changes in this area.
"All parties accept what is the way to the market economy," Krizhinauskas, in Latvian capital Riga for a banking and finance conference, told Reuters in an interview.
"Sometime even for me it is diffcult to find any essential differences (in economic policy)," he said.
Krizhinauskas, who is without party affiliation, said everyone accepted that one day the currency board would be done away with but foresaw no changes in the near future.
The currency board system means the litas' peg of four to one dollar is maintained by the central bank having enough hard currency reserves exactly to back the currency in circulation.
The system also means the central bank is deprived of the powers to maintain the exchange rate through money market intervention or via interest rate changes.
The central bank has said it is working on evaluating the consequences of removing the currency board and returning the bank's powers but Krizhinauskas said such an evaluation would take a long time.
"It is good that they are thinking of alternative ways...but noone will do anything in a short time," he said.
The currency board was introduced to tame soaring inflation and has boosted international and domestic trust in the litas.
But the Homeland Union said it has led to an over-valued currency which has hit exporters.
Under an agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the currency board has to stay until October 1997 but the Homeland Union has hinted it wants to get rid of it before then.
Krizhinauskas said a very gradual dismantling of the system, in a transparent way would do no harm to Lithuania.
But he stressed he saw no immediate action on the issue.
He also said that a dismantling of the currency board did not mean a devaluation of the litas, something that some analysts think will happen if the system is ended.
"Even if Lithuania rejects the currency board, it does not mean that we will devalue the litas," Krizhinauskas said.
